title: Wiggle Subsequence
description: Brute force to optimized: recursively exploring every subsequence versus tracking two running counters (up-ending, down-ending lengths) in one pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: A wiggle sequence is one where consecutive differences strictly alternate between positive and negative (the first difference may be either). Given an integer array nums, return the length of the LONGEST wiggle subsequence (elements need not be contiguous, but must preserve their relative order).

blocks.text: A wiggle subsequence alternates strictly between going up and going down at each step. Only the direction (not the size) of each change matters, so tracking two running counts, the longest wiggle subsequence ending on an "up" move and the longest ending on a "down" move, and updating them as each new element is processed, captures everything needed.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting the Longest Zigzag Path Up and Down a Staircase
blocks.text: Picture walking along a staircase where steps go up and down unevenly, and wanting the longest path where each step strictly alternates direction from the last (up, then down, then up, and so on). Tracking, at each point, "the longest such zigzag ending with an upstep here" and "ending with a downstep here" lets you build the answer incrementally.

blocks.caption: Two running counts, "up" and "down," updated based on whether the current comparison rises or falls

blocks.text: Result: 6. The entire sequence 1,7,4,9,2,5 already alternates up,down,up,down,up perfectly.

Before considering every possible subsequence, notice that only two running quantities are ever needed: the length of the longest wiggle subsequence ending in an "up" move so far, and ending in a "down" move so far, both updateable in O(1) per element as the array is scanned once.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the current element is GREATER than the previous one, any wiggle subsequence ending in a "down" move up to the previous element can be extended by this new "up" move, giving a new candidate "up" length of (previous down length + 1).

Observation 2: Symmetrically, if the current element is SMALLER, any wiggle subsequence ending in an "up" move can be extended by this new "down" move.

Observation 3: If the current element EQUALS the previous one, neither running length changes, since a flat (non-strict) step cannot extend a wiggle sequence.

Observation 4: Maintaining both "up" and "down" running lengths throughout a single pass, and taking their maximum at the end, correctly gives the length of the longest wiggle subsequence.

This leads to a single pass: maintain up and down counters (both starting at 1); for each comparison, update up = down+1 on an increase, or down = up+1 on a decrease. The final answer is the maximum of up and down.
Try every possible subsequence (via subset selection or recursive choice), checking if it strictly alternates up and down, tracking the longest valid one found.

items: Recursively decide, for each element, whether to include it in the subsequence being built.
When including an element, check that it correctly continues the alternating up/down pattern relative to the last included element.
Track the maximum length of any valid wiggle subsequence found across all choices.

codes.python:
def wiggle_max_length_brute(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    best = [1]

    def helper(i, last_val, last_diff, length):
        best[0] = max(best[0], length)
        for j in range(i, n):                             # try including every later element
            diff = nums[j] - last_val
            if diff != 0 and (last_diff == 0 or (diff > 0) != (last_diff > 0)):
                helper(j + 1, nums[j], diff, length + 1)

    for start in range(n):                                    # try every possible starting element
        helper(start + 1, nums[start], 0, 1)
    return best[0]

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every possible subsequence directly implements the definition, guaranteed correct.
This costs exponential time, since every element could be included or excluded, far too slow beyond small inputs.

blocks.text: Limitation: only the direction of each consecutive comparison matters, so tracking two running lengths (up and down) in a single O(n) pass replaces the exponential subsequence search entirely.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why exploring every subsequence is unnecessary: the ONLY thing that matters when extending a wiggle subsequence is whether the next comparison continues the alternation correctly, which is a purely LOCAL, directional fact, not something requiring global subsequence enumeration.

The two-counter DP-like approach: maintain up (longest wiggle subsequence ending in an upswing so far) and down (ending in a downswing so far), both starting at 1 (a single element is trivially both).

Updating the counters: on an increase, up becomes down+1 (extending the best downswing-ending sequence with this new upswing); on a decrease, down becomes up+1 symmetrically; on no change, neither updates.

The core idea: two running counters, updated in O(1) per element based purely on the direction of change, replace the exponential subsequence search.
Maintain up and down counters, both starting at 1. For each consecutive pair, if increasing, set up = down + 1; if decreasing, set down = up + 1. Return max(up, down) at the end.

blocks.caption: Two running counters, updated based purely on the direction of each consecutive comparison

blocks.text: The up and down counters correctly represent the longest wiggle subsequence ending in that direction using only elements seen so far. When a new increase occurs, the best way to extend is from whatever previously ended in a DECREASE (since that correctly continues the alternation), and symmetrically for a decrease extending from a previous increase. Since only the direction of change matters (not any specific values chosen), this local, greedy update at each step correctly builds up the true maximum length without ever needing to consider alternate subsequence choices explicitly.

blocks.text: If the interviewer says "longest alternating up/down subsequence", think: two running counters (up-ending, down-ending lengths), updated based on the direction of each comparison.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Recursive subsequence exploration costs exponential time; the two-counter greedy pass costs O(n) time and O(1) space, the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: two running counters (up-ending, down-ending lengths), updated in O(1) per element based purely on local direction.
Core Idea: on an increase, up becomes down+1; on a decrease, down becomes up+1; the answer is the max of both at the end.
Time: exponential for recursive subsequence exploration, O(n) for the optimized two-counter pass.
Space: O(n) recursion depth versus O(1) extra.
Most Important Observation: only the direction of each local comparison matters, letting two running counters replace full subsequence enumeration.
Interview Difficulty: an elegant, accessible greedy/DP hybrid problem.
One line memory trick: up = down+1 on increase; down = up+1 on decrease; answer is the max.
